title: Concurrency vs parallelism
description: Understand the difference between concurrency and parallelism, and when to use each approach.

data.text: Concurrency and parallelism sound similar, but they solve different problems. Concurrency is about structure — dealing with many things at once by switching between them. Parallelism is about execution — doing many things at the same time on multiple CPU cores. Both are essential for writing fast, responsive software.

Concurrency means your program is designed to handle multiple tasks, even if it only executes one at a time. A single-core CPU can run a web server that handles thousands of requests by rapidly switching between them. The user perceives all requests as happening at once, but the CPU is actually time-slicing.

Parallelism means your program actually runs multiple tasks at the same time on different CPU cores. To benefit from parallelism, your tasks must be independent enough to run simultaneously without constantly waiting for each other. Parallelism only helps if you have enough CPU cores and the workload can be split.

cards.title: Concurrency
cards.description: Dealing with many tasks at once through interleaving. Works on a single core.

cards.title: Parallelism
cards.description: Executing many tasks at the same time on multiple cores. Requires independent work.

data.title: Practical examples
items: A web server uses concurrency to handle many simultaneous client connections
A video editor uses parallelism to render multiple frames at once
A desktop app uses concurrency to keep the UI responsive while loading data
A data pipeline uses parallelism to process large datasets faster

data.title: Parallelism has limits
data.text: Adding more threads does not always make code faster. Beyond a certain point, threads spend more time coordinating than doing useful work. This is called Amdahl's Law.

data.text: The best systems use concurrency to stay responsive and parallelism to maximize throughput. Thread pools, async/await patterns, and message-passing architectures help you write code that works well on both single-core and multi-core machines without rewriting the logic.

items.text: Avoid shared mutable state between concurrent tasks
Use thread-safe data structures or synchronization primitives
Prefer message passing or immutable data over locks
Measure before optimizing — profiling tells you where parallelism actually helps

items.question: Can you have parallelism without concurrency?
items.answer: Technically yes, but it is rare. If tasks are completely independent and run in parallel, you might not think of them as concurrent. In practice, parallelism is a subset of concurrent design.

items.question: Does async/await make code parallel?
items.answer: No. Async/await enables concurrency by freeing the thread while waiting. True parallelism requires multiple CPU cores executing code at the same time.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Concurrency is about structure — handling many tasks at once
Parallelism is about execution — doing many tasks simultaneously
Single-core systems can be concurrent but not parallel
Good design uses concurrency for responsiveness and parallelism for throughput
data.takeaway: Concurrency keeps your program responsive; parallelism makes it faster. Both require careful design to avoid race conditions and deadlocks.
